title: Underwater Volcanoes
objective: After this level you can explain seamounts and volcanic islands.
summary: Seamounts are underwater mountains at least 1,000 m tall, mostly extinct volcanoes. One that grows tall enough becomes an island, like Surtsey in 1963; guyots are old islands planed flat and sunk.

cards.headline: In November 1963, a brand-new island rose out of the Atlantic.
cards.body: Off Iceland's south coast, an eruption that began on the sea floor, about 130 m down, broke through the waves. The new island was named Surtsey. Before it was an island, it was an underwater volcano. The sea floor has plenty of those.

cards.headline: A hundred thousand hidden peaks
cards.body: An underwater mountain with steep sides that rises at least 1,000 m above the surrounding sea floor is a seamount. Most are extinct volcanoes. Scientists estimate there are more than 100,000 of them, and less than one-tenth of a percent have been explored. Put another way: for every thousand seamounts, fewer than one has had a proper visit.

cards.headline: When a volcano breaks the surface
cards.body: Surtsey shows how a volcanic island is born: an eruption on the sea floor keeps building until the volcano pokes above the waves. Its eruptions lasted about three and a half years. Then the sea started pushing back. By 2008, waves had worn away almost half of its area. Building an island takes years; the ocean never stops sanding it down.

cards.headline: Islands that sank
cards.body: Some seamounts have oddly flat tops. These guyots began as volcanic islands near the crests of mid-ocean ridges, where waves planed their summits flat. As the sea floor moved away from the ridge, it sank and carried them down; most of their summits now lie 1,000 to 2,000 m deep. A guyot is a drowned island still wearing the waves' haircut.

cards.headline: Underwater volcanoes: surveyed
learned: Seamounts rise at least 1,000 m; most are extinct volcanoes
Surtsey broke the surface in November 1963
Guyots: old islands, planed flat and sunk

questions.prompt: What makes an underwater mountain count as a seamount?

options.label: It rises at least 1,000 m above the floor around it
Its peak breaks the surface as an island
It sits inside a deep ocean trench
options.rationale: Seamounts rise from the floor; location doesn't define them.

questions.explanation: A seamount is a steep-sided underwater mountain rising at least 1,000 m above the surrounding sea floor.

questions.prompt: Guyots sit 1,000 to 2,000 m underwater. Why do they have flat tops?

options.label: Deep currents slowly scraped them flat
options.rationale: The flattening happened at the surface.

options.label: They formed flat, like lava pancakes
options.rationale: They began as volcanic islands with peaks.

options.label: Waves planed them flat when they were islands, then they sank
Ice sheets once ground them down
options.rationale: Waves, not ice, did the planing.

questions.explanation: Guyots began as volcanic islands whose tops were planed flat by waves before the sinking sea floor carried them down.

questions.prompt: Most seamounts are extinct volcanoes. From Level 13, which undersea feature is the largest single volcanic feature on Earth?

options.label: The Mariana Trench
options.rationale: A trench is a gash, not a volcano.

options.label: The continental shelf
options.rationale: Shelves are continent edges, not volcanoes.

options.label: Surtsey
options.rationale: Surtsey is one small volcanic island.

questions.explanation: The mid-ocean ridge, made of thousands of volcanoes, is the largest single volcanic feature on Earth.
